French adstrate: centuries of Burgundian/French influence in S. Netherlands; cf. van der Wal (2008)

notes: Standard Dutch (ABN / Algemeen Nederlands). ⟨g⟩ realisation is [ɣ] in northern NL and [x] in southern NL / Flanders. /r/ is highly variable. FINAL DEVOICING: b/d/g/v/z devoiced in coda and word-finally. G: voiced [ɣ] onset, voiceless [x] coda — northern Dutch. H: breathy [ɦ]; fully silent in southern dialects. Sources: van Oostendorp (2000), Gussenhoven (1992), Booij (1995). COMPOUND-FINAL SECONDARY STRESS (Booij 1995, ch. 5): non-head members of a compound carry secondary stress and resist the unstressed e -> schwa reduction that a plain unstressed syllable undergoes; the closed set of toponymic/compound-final graphemes ⟨berg⟩/⟨veld⟩/⟨kerk⟩/⟨brecht⟩ is pinned to its unreduced [ɛ] realisation for this reason (Aalbert-style ⟨bert⟩ was left out: wikipron gold is split roughly evenly between [ɛrt] compound forms and [ərt] given-name forms, so no closed rule is safely citable there). ⟨berg⟩/⟨veld⟩ are positionally scoped (positional_graphemes, word_final vs. default) rather than plain unconditional graphemes: a plain grapheme maximal-munch matches inside ordinary inflected forms too (bergen, velden), where the ⟨g⟩/⟨d⟩ is NOT in coda (onset of the following syllable) and must stay voiced per the regular g/d positional rules above -- only word-final ⟨berg⟩/⟨veld⟩ get the devoiced [x]/[t]. ⟨kerk⟩/⟨brecht⟩ need no such split: ⟨k⟩ and ⟨ch⟩ never alternate in Dutch, so the same surface form is correct word-finally and word-internally (kerken, Hubrecht). The adjectival/toponymic suffix ⟨isch⟩ ([-is], ⟨ch⟩ silent, per the existing word-final ⟨sch⟩ -> [s] rule) is likewise pinned as a fixed grapheme rather than derived, since it is a single closed morpheme. HETEROMORPHEMIC ⟨tj⟩ (Booij 1995, ch. 2-3): the digraph ⟨tj⟩ was previously pinned to a single palatalized/affricate segment ([tʲ]/[tʃ]); WikiPron gold shows this is wrong for the overwhelming majority of ⟨tj⟩ words, both the productive diminutive suffix -tje/-etje attached after a stem-final plosive (katje, potje, witje: coda /t/ + suffix onset /j/ across the morpheme boundary, no coalescence) and word-initial ⟨tj-⟩ placenames (Tjalk, Tjonge): [tj], not [tʲ]. The digraph entry was removed so ⟨tj⟩ falls through to the plain ⟨t⟩+⟨j⟩ graphemes, which also fixes a second-order bug: the coalesced digraph was counted as a single intervocalic consonant by the open-syllable-lengthening rule, wrongly lengthening the stem vowel (witje -> *[ʋiːtʲə] instead of [ʋɪtjə]) because tj is phonemically two segments (a closed syllable), not one. A handful of Frisian-influenced placenames (Tjerkgaast, Tjalhuizum) keep an affricate [tʃ] in gold; that minority variant is lexical, not ruled out here. HETEROMORPHEMIC vs TAUTOMORPHEMIC ⟨tj⟩ (word_exceptions, Booij 1995 ch. 2-3 + WikiPron gold): a small closed set of Malay/Indonesian loanwords (ketjap-family: tjap "seal/brand", tjappen, tjaffelen, tjanten, tjetten, tjaptjoi, tjauwmin, tjokvol, matjok, nestje) and Frisian-influenced placenames (Tietjerk, Tjalhuizum, Tjerkgaast, Tjerkwerd) keep ⟨tj⟩ as the coalesced affricate [tʃ] the general rule above no longer produces, because in these words ⟨tj⟩ is TAUTOMORPHEMIC (one morpheme, one syllable onset) rather than the productive diminutive/placename-compound boundary the general rule targets. This is a closed irregular set per AGENTS.md 2 ("a closed irregular set -> word_exceptions; a productive pattern -> the rule layer"), not a general grapheme rule, since the vast majority of ⟨tj⟩ tokens (diminutives, word-initial placenames like Tjalk/Tjonge) are the plain [tj] sequence. "ketjap" and "tjalk" were deliberately NOT added: WikiPron records both the [tj] and [tʃ] pronunciation as attested variants of "ketjap" (multi-reference scoring already credits either), and "tjalk" is genuinely ambiguous at the same lowercased key -- the placename "Tjalk" (Friesland) is gold [tj] while the common noun "tjalk" (a sailing barge) is gold [tʃ]; a single override cannot satisfy both senses, so the word is left on the general (majority, placename-consistent) rule. OPEN-SYLLABLE LENGTHENING/TENSING: Open-syllable lengthening / tensing (Booij 1995, ch. 2, and Gussenhoven 1999, JIPA Illustration of Dutch): a single vowel letter is read as the TENSE vowel in an open syllable (ma-ken, lo-pen, u-ren, li-ter) and as the LAX vowel in a closed one (mak-ken, lop, ur-nen, lip). Keyed on syllable APERTURE, so the spec's own syllabifier -- onset-constrained for Dutch -- decides it: a-bri-koos and a-cro-baat have an open first syllable because /br/ and /kr/ are legal Dutch onsets. SHORT TENSE HIGH VOWELS (Booij 1995, ch. 2; Gussenhoven 1999, JIPA Illustration of Dutch): Dutch /i y u/ -- spelt ⟨ie⟩ ⟨uu⟩ ⟨oe⟩ and the open-syllable readings of ⟨i⟩ ⟨u⟩ -- are tense but SHORT, not long; only /eː øː oː aː/ are long. /i/ and /y/ lengthen before /r/ (NL_HIGH_TENSE_LENGTHENING_BEFORE_R_I/_Y). /u/ does NOT: although Booij states the lengthening for the whole series, WikiPron gold is 5.8:1 AGAINST it (78 [uːr] to 450 [ur]) -- boer [bur], aanvoer [aːnvur], beroerd [bərurt] -- and adding the /u/ member measured PER 0.0902 -> 0.0910, WER 0.4444 -> 0.4486 on nl wikipron. The rule is therefore stated per-vowel, not for the series.

stress.notes: Germanic initial stress default (Booij 1995, ch. 5); the -e(n) verbal/plural ending is unstressed, which is what the open/closed-syllable vowel-length rule and the e -> schwa reduction below need.

allophone_rules.notes: Regressive devoicing assimilation (Booij 1995, ch. 2 sec. 2.5): Dutch obstruents in coda devoice not only word-finally but also before a following voiceless obstruent within the word, e.g. zeg-t [zɛxt], lieg-t [liːxt], hoog-te [ɦoːxtə]. The existing word_final positional override for ⟨g⟩ handles the absolute-final case; this rule extends the same devoicing to pre-obstruent coda position without touching ⟨g⟩ before a sonorant/vowel (dag-je stays [ɣ]: j is not an obstruent).

Unstressed tense vowel (Booij 1995, ch. 2): an unstressed word-final ⟨i⟩ surfaces tense-but-short [i], not lax [ɪ] -- Ali [aːli], Adri [aːdri]. Mirrors the analogous German DE_UNSTRESSED_TENSE_*_FINAL rules (final unstressed high/mid vowels resist laxing).

Unstressed tense vowel in hiatus (Booij 1995, ch. 2): an unstressed ⟨i⟩ directly before another vowel letter (Aziaat, Ariër, Adriaan, -ië/-iër loanword endings) surfaces tense-but-short [i], not lax [ɪ]; the hiatus context blocks the closed-syllable laxing that a following consonant would trigger.

The tense high vowels /i, y, u/ are phonologically SHORT in Dutch -- unlike the long mid vowels /eː, øː, oː/ (Booij 1995, ch. 2; Gussenhoven 1999, JIPA Illustration of Dutch, transcribes them [i] [y] [u]). Booij states lengthening before /r/ for the series; WikiPron gold bears it out for /i/ and /y/ but REFUTES it for /u/, so the series is split into per-vowel rules rather than applied wholesale. For /i/ gold runs 703 [iːr] to 349 [ir] (2.0:1 FOR lengthening): banier [baːniːr], bankier [bɑŋkiːr], aasgier [aːsxiːr]. Measured on nl wikipron, removing this rule alone costs PER 0.0902 -> 0.0905 and WER 0.4446 -> 0.4490 (measured on the post-#850 tree).

Measured on nl wikipron, removing this rule alone costs PER 0.0902 -> 0.0908 and WER 0.4446 -> 0.4503 (measured on the post-#850 tree).

Regressive devoicing assimilation (Booij 1995, ch. 2 sec. 2.5): a Dutch obstruent in coda devoices before a following voiceless obstruent, not only word-finally -- raad-sel [raːtsəl], web-site, lief-st, rei-zt. The rule is stated for the whole obstruent series; ⟨g⟩ already had it (NL_CODA_DEVOICE_G) and the remaining voiced obstruents ⟨b d v z⟩ follow the same generalisation.
